title: We Need More Sustainable Packaging, Like, Yesterday
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss packaging waste, focusing on plastic. They cover US municipal solid waste statistics (packaging recycling rates for plastic, aluminum, and cardboard), the history of reuse before garbage pickup, early packaging innovations (corrugated cardboard, single-serve foods, the plastic grocery bag), and the McDonald's shift to single-use packaging. They discuss Amazon's packaging and ocean plastic, meal kit packaging, Charm-style hard-to-recycle drop-offs, and alternative materials like PLA corn plastic, mycelium (mushroom) packaging, and algae/seaweed plastics, including the Tom Ford plastic alternatives prize. The episode closes with extended producer responsibility (EPR) and the polluter pays principle, India's recycling credit system, California's packaging law, state-level plastic bag bans and preemption laws, and the downsides of cotton totes. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about not deferring breaks, followed by the sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and packaging anecdotes
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the show's environmental episodes, Crown Royal packaging, smaller COVID test boxes, and excessive plastic packaging on tools.

segments.title: Packaging waste statistics
segments.summary: The hosts say packaging makes up a large share of municipal solid waste and cite recycling figures: about a tenth of packaging was recycled in 1960, plastic is the biggest problem with about 10 million tons landfilled, aluminum cans and cardboard fare differently.

segments.title: Plastic packaging and tamper-proof wrap
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss single-use plastic forms like wrappers and styrofoam peanuts, and how shrink wrap and tamper-proof packaging spread after the Tylenol poisonings, plus frustrating tool packaging.

segments.title: Pre-industrial reuse and early garbage history
segments.summary: The hosts recall relatives who reused and composted and had no garbage pickup, discuss water glass repairs, and note 18th-century garbage dumping into the East River.

segments.title: Packaging innovations and early single-use history
segments.summary: The hosts cover corrugated cardboard invented in England in 1856 replacing wooden crates, Nabisco's single-serve packages, Kellogg's cereal box, beer can history, and wetland dumps such as Boston's Back Bay and Staten Island's Fresh Kills landfill.

segments.title: Plastic grocery bags and the rise of single-use
segments.summary: The hosts describe the plastic garbage bag campaign, the plastic grocery bag appearing in the 1960s and the cost comparison that drove adoption, the plastic industry's reuse claims, and the 1986 General Federation of Women's Clubs opposition.

segments.title: McDonald's packaging and a break
segments.summary: The hosts note McDonald's pioneered single-use food packaging and later dropped its polystyrene clamshell (McDLT) packaging, then transition to a break.

segments.title: Amazon shipping packaging and ocean plastic
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Amazon's shipping volume, a report by Oceanica on plastic packaging reaching waterways, plastic film air pillows, and recycling plastic bags at grocery stores; they also praise Charm, a hard-to-recycle drop-off center in Atlanta.

segments.title: Meal kit packaging
segments.summary: The hosts weigh meal kit services' heavy packaging against reduced food waste, citing a 2019 study finding Blue Apron had lower emissions than grocery store equivalents.

segments.title: Alternative packaging materials
segments.summary: The hosts discuss PLA corn-based plastic that requires industrial composting, corn packing peanuts and food-crop competition, mycelium packaging grown from fungi, and algae or seaweed plastics including Tom Ford's plastic alternatives prize with five of eight finalists using algae or seaweed.

segments.title: Policy: EPR, polluter pays, and plastic bag bans
segments.summary: The hosts explain extended producer responsibility and the polluter pays principle, India's recycling credit system, California's packaging law, the multi-state EPR coalition, state plastic bag bans and preemption laws, and the downsides of cotton totes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode with a sign-off. Listener mail from Tony about not deferring breaks is read earlier in the episode.
